fields.h1: The Marks of a True Revival
fields.meta_title: The Marks of a True Revival: How to Tell the Real Thing
fields.description: Not everything that calls itself revival is the real thing. Here are the Scriptural marks by which to tell a true revival from a passing excitement.
fields.body_html:
Not everything that calls itself revival is the real thing, and not everything strange or emotional is false. From the beginning, seasons of unusual spiritual stirring have drawn both genuine works of God and counterfeits — and sincere believers have disagreed sharply about which is which. So how do you tell a true revival from a passing excitement, or from something worse? Scripture does not leave us to guess. It gives clear tests, and John’s blunt command governs them all: “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

The point of these tests is not to make us cynical about anything unusual, nor gullible about anything intense. It is to help us discern the fruit. A true revival can look messy at the edges and still be a mighty work of God; a false one can look impressive and be empty. What follows are the enduring marks by which Scripture — and the wisest observers of past awakenings — have discerned the genuine article.

It exalts Jesus Christ

The surest mark of the Spirit’s work is that he glorifies Christ. Jesus said of the Spirit, “He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14). Where the Spirit is truly at work, Jesus is magnified — his person loved, his cross treasured, his lordship confessed. Paul makes the same point a test of authenticity: “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

So ask of any movement: what does it do to people’s estimate of Christ? A genuine revival leaves men and women in love with the Saviour, ashamed of having thought little of him, eager to obey and adore him. If the attention settles instead on a personality, an experience, a set of phenomena, or the excitement itself — if Christ becomes a means to some other end rather than the end of all desire — then whatever is happening, it is not chiefly the Spirit of God, for the Spirit’s whole delight is to make Jesus glorious.

This single test quietly settles many questions. A stirring may be noisy or quiet, sudden or gradual, accompanied by strong emotion or none; but if, when it passes, people love and treasure Christ more than they did before, God has been at work. The Spirit is not given to advertise himself, nor to draw a crowd to a preacher, nor to leave people fascinated with their own experiences. He comes, always, to make the Son beautiful in the eyes of sinners — and a movement can be measured by nothing more surely than whether that is what it does.

It works against sin and toward holiness

The Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, and his coming makes people holy — not merely happy. A true revival produces a piercing sense of the sinfulness of sin, and then a war against it. Jesus gave the plainest test of all: “you will recognize them by their fruits... every healthy tree bears good fruit” (Matthew 7:16–17). Not by their gifts, their crowds, or their feelings, but by their fruit.

This is why the truest evidence of revival is unglamorous and moral: repentance, restitution, reconciliation, honesty, purity, generosity, forgiveness of old wrongs. In the East African Revival, the mark of the “saved ones” was not spectacle but confession and changed lives — stolen goods returned, enemies embraced, hidden sins brought into the light. Where a stirring leaves people tender about sin and hungry for holiness, God is at work. Where it leaves them excited but unchanged — or worse, proud and careless about obedience — the tree is telling the truth about the root.

It deepens love for the Scriptures and for truth

The Spirit who inspired the Scriptures never leads people away from them. John gives a searching test: “Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (1 John 4:6). A genuine work of God sends people back to the Bible with fresh hunger, submits itself to the Bible’s authority, and grows in a love of the truth as it is.

Counterfeit stirrings, by contrast, tend to drift from Scripture toward novelty, private revelations, or teachers who tickle the ears. Paul’s instruction holds the balance perfectly: “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). We are neither to smother what God is doing nor to swallow everything uncritically, but to weigh it all by the Word — welcoming the fire while refusing the false.

It produces love for God and for one another

The Spirit’s chief fruit is love. Where he moves, walls come down: between God and the sinner, and between the estranged. John writes, “let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God” (1 John 4:7). And Paul’s famous list begins there: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

A true revival is known by a sudden warmth of love — for God, whom the awakened soul now adores, and for people, including those it once despised. Old feuds are healed. Races and classes that kept apart find themselves reconciled at the foot of the cross. If a movement breeds division, pride, contempt, or a party spirit, its fruit is exposing it. But where hard hearts grow tender and enemies become family, the Spirit of love is unmistakably present.

What a counterfeit looks like

It helps to see the false thing clearly, so we are not deceived by it and not frightened of the true thing that resembles it at the edges. A counterfeit revival typically cries peace where there is no peace, promising blessing while leaving sin comfortably in place — the very thing Jeremiah rebuked: “They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). It offers the excitement of religion without its cost, and a “gospel” that never confronts the conscience.

Paul warned of a religion with “the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5) — all form and no fire, or all fire and no fruit. Counterfeits also tend to gather around a man rather than the Master, to prize the sensational over the holy, and to leave behind, when the excitement fades, no lasting change in how people live. None of this means we should treat every unusual thing with suspicion. Gamaliel’s wisdom still stands: if a work “is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them” (Acts 5:38–39). The test of time will expose the counterfeit and vindicate the true. What we must not do is bless the false for its energy, or reject the true for its strangeness. We test, and we wait, and we watch the fruit.

Emotion is not the enemy — nor the evidence

Some distrust any revival because it involves deep feeling; others treat feeling itself as proof. Both are mistaken. Jonathan Edwards, who watched a great awakening at close range and thought harder about it than perhaps anyone, put the matter memorably: “True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.” The heart, moved toward God, is not incidental to real faith; it is near the center of it.

True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections.Jonathan Edwards

But Edwards was equally clear that raised affections, tears, and dramatic experiences prove nothing by themselves. The question is always what the emotion produces. Does it humble or inflate? Does it lead to lasting obedience or evaporate by the weekend? Genuine revival often carries strong emotion — deep weeping over sin, overflowing joy in Christ — but the emotion is the effect of seeing God truly, not the thing to be chased. Measure by fruit, not by feeling.

Its lasting fruit is a changed church and a reached world

Finally, a true revival is proved over time by what it leaves behind. Luke’s portrait of the Pentecostal church is the template: “they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers... And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:42, 47). Enduring devotion to the Word, to fellowship, to prayer; and an overflow of witness that draws in the lost. Real awakenings leave the church more prayerful, more holy, more united, and more evangelistic for a generation — not merely a memory of an exciting few weeks.

So we need not be naïve, and we need not be afraid. When God visits his people, the marks are recognizable: Christ exalted, sin hated, Scripture loved, love poured out, and a lasting harvest gathered. Test the spirits, hold fast what is good, and thank God for every genuine work of his hand — for a church that can discern the real thing is a church ready to receive it.
